scenes.sub: Write the code once. The compiler writes a version for each type.
scenes.say: What are templates? They let you write a function or class once, with the type as a parameter. The compiler then generates the real code for each type you use.

scenes.head: One function, any type
scenes.say: Without templates you'd write max for int, again for double, again for string. With a template, T is a placeholder type. Call maxOf with two ints, and the compiler deduces T is int. Two doubles, T is double. You can also spell it out in angle brackets. A classic gotcha: an int and a double. T can't be both, so deduction fails and it won't compile.

scenes.head: Instantiation happens at compile time
scenes.say: The template itself is a recipe, not code. When you use it, the compiler stamps out a separate function: one for int, one for double, one for string. This is called instantiation. It all happens at compile time, so there's no runtime cost. The price is longer builds and bigger binaries. Because the compiler needs the full recipe at each use, templates usually live in header files.

scenes.head: Class templates
scenes.say: Classes can be templates too. Box of int and Box of string are two completely different types, generated from one definition. The whole S T L is built this way: vector, map, unique pointer. This is called generic programming. And unlike Java generics, each instantiation is real, type specific code.

lines: Templates: code parameterized by type (or value), written once.
The compiler instantiates a separate version per type, at compile time.
Zero runtime cost; costs compile time and binary size. Defined in headers.
